thread.title: 'Let's depoliticize it': Commission recommends routine property assessments in Allegheny County - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: 'Let's depoliticize it': Commission recommends routine property assessments in Allegheny County - NewsBreak

author: Ada Perlman
title: 'Let's depoliticize it': Commission recommends routine property assessments in Allegheny County - NewsBreak
text:
By Ada Perlman ,
8 hours ago Rowhomes in the mostly renter-occupied neighborhood of South Oakland. (Photo by Stephanie Strasburg/Public Source) Routine property reassessments may soon become the norm in Allegheny County.
The county’s Government Review Commission on Wednesday released a draft report section on property assessment and taxation, recommending routine assessments every four years in line with the county executive election cycle.
The current absence of a timeline for statewide or countywide routine reassessments has created a system of delayed reassessments and inequities . Some homeowners and school districts have sued the county over disputed values. The last countywide assessment was conducted in 2013.
“Let’s depoliticize it and make it routine,” said Rohit Acharya, chair of the commission.
Property assessments determine the value of homes and other buildings to help the county calculate how much residents pay each year in county, school and municipal taxes.
Commission member William McKain said the long gaps between reassessments in the past has created “tension and misinformation,” contributing to resident anxiety.
The nine-person Government Review Commission is an independent body appointed by the Allegheny County Council and County Executive Sara Innamorato. Its role is to advise the county government, but its recommendations are not binding.
The Allegheny County Government Review Commission recommended routine property reassessments in a public meeting on Aug. 12, 2026. (Photo by Ada Perlman/Pittsburgh’s Public Source) Innamorato said in a statement she and her team would review the recommendation in the coming days.
“Public education and engagement, protection for homeowners, and providing a predictable and responsible timeline for routine reassessments are necessary for making reassessment a regular function of County government,” her statement said.
The commission’s vote reflects Innamorato’s promise to work on establishing regular property reassessments during her campaign in 2023 .
Mike Suley, chair of the property assessment appeals board and a vocal critic of the way local assessments have been handled, said he was pleased to see the county government supporting routine reassessments.
“You can’t appeal your way to fairness, you have to do it through the county,” he said.
Acharya said the commission chose to release the Property Assessment and Taxation section of its broader annual report earlier than the rest because of the “consequential decisions” being considered by county council amid debates on adopting routine property assessment and multiple pending lawsuits from county residents.
The draft’s recommendations are organized into 14 sections, including new assessment practices, education recommendations, and impact of taxation around the county.
The commission emphasized the need for resident input in the reassessment process, which includes using “plain language notices, visual examples, and town halls.”
“When you educate, you take away the fear and uncertainty,” said commission member Gretchen Moore.
Among its recommendations, the commission also suggested that the county “explore modernizing the assessment process” through new technologies, such as aerial imagery and flyovers.
Acharya said these technologies can reduce the administrative burden of conducting assessments, something other municipalities are exploring across the county .
Pennsylvania is the only state in the country that does not require routine property reassessments, according to a legislative memo written by state Sen. Wayne Fontana, D-Brookline. Fontana has proposed legislation that would require every county in the state to have routine property reassessments, which the commission voted to support.
“Almost every county in the country does this already and they do it in a consistent way. It’s time. It has to move forward,” said commission member Matthew Barron. “This is about building a county that is going to be healthy and is going to be there for the future.”
Ada Perlman is an editorial intern at Pittsburgh’s Public Source. She can be reached at ada@publicsource.org .
Jamie Wiggan contributed reporting.
